rdp_config.name: RDP Config
rdp_config.command: $deny = (Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' -Name fDenyTSConnections -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).fDenyTSConnections; if ($deny -eq 1 -or $null -eq $deny) { 'RDP_DISABLED' } else { $rdp = Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp' -Name UserAuthentication, SecurityLayer -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; "fDenyTSConnections=$deny"; "UserAuthentication=$($rdp.UserAuthentication)"; "SecurityLayer=$($rdp.SecurityLayer)" }

rules.name: RDP Network Level Authentication enabled (or RDP disabled)
rules.finding: RDP Network Level Authentication not required
rules.explanation: RDP is enabled but Network Level Authentication (NLA) is not required, allowing unauthenticated users to reach the login screen and attempt brute-force attacks.
rules.remediation: Enable NLA: Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp' UserAuthentication 1. Or disable RDP entirely if unused.

openssh_config.name: OpenSSH Config
openssh_config.command: if (Get-Service sshd -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) { Get-Content "$env:ProgramData\ssh\sshd_config" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-String -Pattern 'PermitRootLogin|PasswordAuthentication|PubkeyAuthentication|MaxAuthTries' | Out-String } else { 'NOT_INSTALLED' }

listening_ports.name: Listening Ports
listening_ports.command: Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 200

firewall.name: Windows Firewall
firewall.command: Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction, DefaultOutboundAction | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 200

rules.name: Windows Firewall is enabled on all profiles
rules.finding: Windows Firewall disabled on one or more profiles
rules.explanation: Windows Firewall is disabled on one or more network profiles (Domain, Private, Public), leaving the server unprotected.
rules.remediation: Enable Windows Firewall: Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -Enabled True

local_admins.name: Local Administrators
local_admins.command: Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, ObjectClass, PrincipalSource | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 200

rules.name: Guest account is disabled
rules.explanation: The built-in Guest account is enabled, providing anonymous access to the system.
rules.remediation: Disable the guest account: Disable-LocalUser -Name Guest

password_policy.name: Password Policy
password_policy.command: $tmp = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName(); try { secedit /export /areas SECURITYPOLICY /cfg $tmp /quiet | Out-Null; Get-Content $tmp -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_ -match '^\s*(MinimumPasswordLength|LockoutBadCount|PasswordComplexity|MaximumPasswordAge|PasswordHistorySize)\s*=' } } catch { 'EXPORT_FAILED' } finally { Remove-Item $tmp -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }

rules.name: Minimum password length at least 14 characters
rules.explanation: Minimum password length is set below 14 characters, making passwords easier to brute-force.
rules.remediation: Set MinimumPasswordLength to 14 via Group Policy or: secedit /configure with an INF containing 'MinimumPasswordLength = 14'.

rules.name: Account lockout threshold configured
rules.explanation: No account lockout threshold is set (LockoutBadCount=0), allowing unlimited brute-force attempts.
rules.remediation: Set LockoutBadCount to a positive value (e.g. 5) via Group Policy or secedit.

rules.name: Password complexity enabled
rules.explanation: Password complexity is disabled, allowing simple dictionary-based passwords.
rules.remediation: Enable password complexity via Group Policy or secedit: 'PasswordComplexity = 1'.

rules.name: Windows Defender real-time protection enabled
rules.explanation: Windows Defender real-time protection is disabled, leaving the server vulnerable to malware.
rules.remediation: Enable real-time protection: Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false

rules.name: Windows Defender antivirus enabled
rules.explanation: Windows Defender antivirus is not enabled. The server has no active malware protection.
rules.remediation: Enable Windows Defender via Group Policy or Security Center.

rules.name: Windows Defender signatures updated within the last 7 days
rules.finding: Windows Defender signatures older than 7 days
rules.explanation: Windows Defender malware definitions are older than 7 days. Stale signatures miss current threats.
rules.remediation: Force an immediate signature update: Update-MpSignature. Ensure the Windows Update service is enabled and the host can reach Microsoft update servers.

security_updates.name: Security Updates
security_updates.command: $Session = New-Object -ComObject Microsoft.Update.Session; $Searcher = $Session.CreateUpdateSearcher(); try { $Results = $Searcher.Search('IsInstalled=0 and Type="Software"'); if ($Results.Updates.Count -eq 0) { 'No security updates available' } else { "$($Results.Updates.Count) updates available"; $Results.Updates | Select-Object -First 10 -ExpandProperty Title } } catch { 'Windows Update check failed' }

rules.name: No pending security updates
rules.explanation: Windows updates are available but not installed, leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched.
rules.remediation: Install pending updates via Windows Update or WSUS.

failed_logins.name: Failed Logins (24h)
failed_logins.command: $since = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24); try { (Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=$since} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object).Count } catch { '0' }

rules.name: Failed logins under 100 in 24h
rules.explanation: Over 100 failed login attempts in the last 24 hours, indicating a brute-force attack or misconfigured client.
rules.remediation: Investigate source of failed logins in Event Viewer (Security log, Event ID 4625). Consider enabling account lockout policy.

audit_policy.name: Audit Policy
audit_policy.command: $gpocsv = Join-Path $env:SystemRoot 'System32\GroupPolicy\Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\Audit\audit.csv'; if (Test-Path $gpocsv) { $row = Import-Csv $gpocsv | Where-Object { $_.'Subcategory GUID' -eq '{0CCE9215-69AE-11D9-BED3-505054503030}' }; if ($row -and $row.'Setting Value') { "Logon_SettingValue=$($row.'Setting Value')" } else { 'Logon_SettingValue=0' } } else { 'Logon_SettingValue=unknown' }; auditpol /get /category:* 2>$null | Out-String -Width 200

rules.name: Logon events auditing enabled (Success + Failure)
rules.finding: Logon events auditing not enabled (Success + Failure)
rules.explanation: Logon event auditing (subcategory {0CCE9215-69AE-11D9-BED3-505054503030}) is not configured for both Success and Failure. Attack detection and incident response depend on these events.
rules.remediation: Enable via auditpol (English): auditpol /set /subcategory:{0CCE9215-69AE-11D9-BED3-505054503030} /success:enable /failure:enable. Or set via GPO: Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration → Logon/Logoff → Logon = Success and Failure.

rules.name: SMB signing required
rules.explanation: SMB signing is not required, making the server vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks on file sharing.
rules.remediation: Enable required SMB signing: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force

service_accounts.name: Service Accounts
service_accounts.command: Get-WmiObject Win32_Service | Where-Object { $_.StartName -and $_.StartName -ne 'LocalSystem' -and $_.StartName -ne 'NT AUTHORITY\LocalService' -and $_.StartName -ne 'NT AUTHORITY\NetworkService' -and $_.StartName -ne 'NT Authority\LocalService' -and $_.StartName -ne 'NT Authority\NetworkService' } | Select-Object Name, StartName, State | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 200

tls_protocols.name: TLS Protocols
tls_protocols.command: foreach ($proto in @('SSL 2.0','SSL 3.0','TLS 1.0','TLS 1.1','TLS 1.2','TLS 1.3')) { $path = "HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\Protocols\$proto\Server"; $enabled = (Get-ItemProperty -Path $path -Name Enabled -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Enabled; if ($null -eq $enabled) { "$proto : Default" } elseif ($enabled -eq 0) { "$proto : Disabled" } else { "$proto : Enabled" } }

rules.name: No weak TLS protocols (SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1)
rules.finding: Weak TLS protocols enabled (SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1)
rules.explanation: Weak TLS/SSL protocols are explicitly enabled in the registry. These are vulnerable to known attacks (POODLE, BEAST).
rules.remediation: Disable weak protocols via registry: set Enabled=0 under HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\Protocols\<version>\Server

rules.name: SMB1 protocol disabled
rules.explanation: SMB1 is an obsolete and insecure file-sharing protocol. It is the attack vector for WannaCry, NotPetya, and EternalBlue. It must be disabled on all modern Windows servers.
rules.remediation: Disable SMB1: Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force. Also remove the feature: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol

rules.name: User Account Control (UAC) enabled
rules.explanation: User Account Control is disabled. UAC is a baseline privilege-escalation barrier — without it, any process running as administrator executes with full privileges, and standard user prompts for elevation are bypassed.
rules.remediation: Enable UAC via registry: Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System' EnableLUA 1. Reboot to apply.

rules.name: WDigest cleartext credential storage disabled
rules.explanation: WDigest can be forced to cache cleartext credentials in LSASS memory, where tools like Mimikatz can harvest them. On modern Windows this is disabled by default but can be re-enabled by attackers or malware.
rules.remediation: Explicitly disable: Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest' UseLogonCredential 0 -Type DWord

rules.name: Automatic login disabled and no default password stored
rules.finding: Automatic login enabled with a stored password
rules.explanation: Automatic login with a stored cleartext password in the registry is enabled. Anyone with local read access to the SAM/Registry can retrieve the credentials, and the host logs in without authentication on reboot.
rules.remediation: Disable autologon: Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' AutoAdminLogon 0. Remove DefaultPassword: Remove-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' DefaultPassword -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

bitlocker.name: BitLocker Volume Encryption
bitlocker.command: $bl = Get-BitLockerVolume -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.VolumeType -eq 'OperatingSystem' -or $_.VolumeType -eq 'FixedData' }; if ($bl) { $bl | ForEach-Object { "Volume=$($_.MountPoint) Type=$($_.VolumeType) Protection=$($_.ProtectionStatus) Encrypt=$($_.EncryptionPercentage)%" } } else { 'NOT_AVAILABLE' }

rules.name: BitLocker protection enabled on fixed volumes
rules.finding: BitLocker protection disabled on one or more fixed volumes
rules.explanation: One or more fixed volumes has BitLocker protection disabled. Physical theft or disposal of the disk exposes all data unencrypted.
rules.remediation: Enable BitLocker on each fixed volume: Enable-BitLocker -MountPoint C: -EncryptionMethod XtsAes256 -UsedSpaceOnly -TpmProtector -ErrorAction Stop. Store recovery keys in a secure offline location (or Entra / Active Directory if joined).

rules.name: Disk encryption (BitLocker) active
rules.explanation: No BitLocker-protected fixed volume detected. Data on disk is not protected if the device is lost, stolen, or decommissioned without proper wiping.
rules.remediation: Enable BitLocker on the OS volume (manage-bde -on C:) and on data volumes. Use a TPM-backed protector and store recovery keys centrally.

powershell_logging.name: PowerShell Logging
powershell_logging.command: $sbl = (Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' -Name EnableScriptBlockLogging -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).EnableScriptBlockLogging; if ($null -eq $sbl) { 'ScriptBlockLogging=unset' } else { "ScriptBlockLogging=$sbl" }; $ml = (Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging' -Name EnableModuleLogging -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).EnableModuleLogging; if ($null -eq $ml) { 'ModuleLogging=unset' } else { "ModuleLogging=$ml" }

rules.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging enabled
rules.finding: PowerShell Script Block Logging not enabled
rules.explanation: PowerShell Script Block Logging is not enabled. Without it, malicious PowerShell activity (common attacker tradecraft) leaves little forensic trace.
rules.remediation: Enable via GPO (Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows PowerShell → Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging) or registry: Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging' EnableScriptBlockLogging 1 -Type DWord -Force. Create the key first if it doesn't exist.

rules.name: LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) disabled
rules.explanation: LLMNR is a legacy name-resolution protocol that is abused by attackers (Responder, Inveigh) to capture NTLMv2 hashes for offline cracking. It is enabled by default on Windows.
rules.remediation: Disable via GPO (Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Network → DNS Client → Turn off multicast name resolution = Enabled) or registry: New-Item 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient' -Force; Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient' EnableMulticast 0 -Type DWord

installed_packages.name: Installed Packages
installed_packages.command: $ErrorActionPreference='SilentlyContinue'; try { pip3 list --format=freeze 2>$null | Where-Object { $_ -match '==' } | ForEach-Object { $p = $_ -split '==',2; 'PyPI' + [char]9 + $p[0] + [char]9 + $p[1] } } catch {}; try { pip list --format=freeze 2>$null | Where-Object { $_ -match '==' } | ForEach-Object { $p = $_ -split '==',2; 'PyPI' + [char]9 + $p[0] + [char]9 + $p[1] } } catch {}
